transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-01-20
Start: 15:00 PST
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Kim, Maya Patel, Luis Ortega (Redwood) — Alex Rivera, Priya Shah, Sam Cole, Dana Li (Nimbus Health)

Auto-generated summary:
Redwood gave a hosted API walkthrough focused on streaming chat and retry/backoff patterns. Customer (Nimbus Health) is evaluating hosted vs dedicated for a clinical summarization assistant; primary concerns were latency, cost per token, and PHI handling. Action items were agreed: Redwood to share pricing + sandbox, SE to share concrete retry patterns and console steps, Nimbus to run a short sandbox and report latency.

Topics discussed:
- Streaming behavior and incremental tokens (SSE/chunking)
- Gen parameters: max_tokens, temperature, top_p, stop sequences
- Retry/backoff strategy and idempotency keys
- Console quick tour: per-route latency and token cost breakdowns
- Basic Optimize suggestions: batching, cache (KV prefix caching) and quantization tradeoffs
- Security: SOC 2, VPC/private deployment options, KMS integrations, audit logs

Action items (in transcript):
- Jordan to email pricing and sandbox link
- Maya to attach streaming retry doc and console screenshots
- Sam to try sandbox and report performance numbers

Transcript body:
[00:00] Jordan (AE): hey everyone thanks for joining, um i think we've got about 45 minutes, we'll do a quick orientation to the hosted api streaming behavior and then show the console and some best practices for retries and params. sound good?
[00:12] Alex (CTO, Nimbus): yeah that sounds great, um our main ask is low latency for interactive docs and also we have PHI so we want to understand retention and encryption flow.
[00:22] Maya (SE): perfect, i'll start with the live demo of a streaming chat call and show how tokens arrive incrementally and where you hook in backoff and reconnect logic.
[00:31] Priya (PM): quick note — timeline for pilot is 2–3 weeks, need to show SLA and cost estimate to execs.
[00:40] Maya: noted. ok i'm sharing my screen, first i run a simple POST to /v1/chat.generate with stream true as a header. the response is server-sent events, you'll see data: chunks with delta tokens. so client gets incremental text and can display typing.
[01:05] Speaker 1 (background): mm-hmm
[01:09] Maya: common pitfall is not handling partial events — do not assume final punctuation until the stream sends done. also watch for duplicate tokens if you reconnect without idempotency keys.
[01:23] Sam (ML Eng): can you explain idempotency keys in more detail? we want to avoid double billing if a retry happens.
[01:29] Maya: yes, Redwood accepts an Idempotency-Key header. attach a request-scoped key; server will dedupe identical payloads for a short TTL. for streaming, if you get a network error, reconnect using the same key and the server will either resume or return a cached final payload depending on model support. this reduces duplicate token charges.
[01:52] Dana (Security): how long is that TTL? and does it persist across restarts?
[01:57] Luis (Redwood): TTL for idempotency is 10 minutes in hosted by default; it survives worker restarts in the control plane but not across long-term model version rollouts. for longer dedupe windows you'd look at session management in your app or a dedicated deployment.
[02:12] Alex: okay that helps, can you show retry/backoff patterns — exponential backoff, jitter, etc? we get intermittent latency spikes.
[02:20] Maya: sure — we recommend three retry attempts with full jitter, base backoff 200ms doubling, cap at 2s. for transient 5xx or network errors, retry. for 4xx like invalid input, do not. for rate-limit (429) return the Retry-After header and backoff accordingly. here's a sample pseudo-code i use.
[02:45] Maya: also note streaming-specific guidance — if a stream closes mid-response, attempt a resume (same idempotency key) rather than a full-fresh request when you expect the same continuation. that keeps latency down and avoids re-generating earlier tokens.
[03:05] Priya: what about partial results and user-visible UX? should we display partial, then replace when final arrives?
[03:11] Jordan: usually show partial as typing cursor, then lock final on done. but be careful if you do local aggregation because that can trigger multiple UI updates and perceived flicker.
[03:23] Maya: moving to model params, common knobs — max_tokens controls the generation length, temperature controls randomness, top_p is nucleus sampling. for deterministic clinical summaries you might use temperature 0–0.2 and smaller max_tokens plus explicit stop sequences.
[03:46] Sam: what about tokens counting? we have long prompts with patient history.
[03:50] Maya: Redwood console shows token breakdown per request — prompt tokens vs completion tokens and cost estimate. for long context use prefix KV cache or chunking + summarization. Optimize suggestions will recommend quantization or smaller model if cost is high and quality acceptable.
[04:18] Alex: is prefix caching available on hosted?
[04:21] Luis: yes, we offer automatic KV prefix caching for repeated conversation starters. you'll see cache hit rates in the console and it reduces completion cost and latency. note for PHI you can opt out of caching or enable customer-managed keys in Private deployment for extra isolation.
[04:41] Priya: can you show the console now? we'd like to see per-route metrics.
[04:46] Maya: switching to console — this is the per-route dashboard. on the left is latency P50/P90, middle is token cost breakdown, right is recent errors with stack traces. this is useful to triage retries vs model slowness.
[05:10] Maya: here's a route filter for our demo route; i can replay a request from the history to show a streaming trace. see how the timeline shows SSE chunks streaming in and the latency for first byte vs total completion.
[05:31] Speaker 2 (crosstalk): wow
[05:33] Sam: regarding model fallbacks — do you support automatic fallback to smaller/faster variants if latency spikes?
[05:38] Luis: yes, smart routing can fallback to a compatible model variant or even a reduced precision quantized profile. you can configure cost vs latency policies per route: prefer low latency, or prefer low cost; it will try the best candidate and fallback if capacity issues occur.
[06:00] Alex: how do we do debugging of partial transcripts? sometimes our downstream QA flagged hallucinations mid-stream.
[06:06] Maya: you can attach a deterministic eval prompt set and run regression tests via Console -> Evals. for runtime, we log token deltas and have a per-token trace you can export for investigation.
[06:20] Priya: security again — SOC 2 and encryption at rest/in transit? we need to map to our infosec checklist.
[06:27] Jordan: Redwood is SOC 2 Type II and you can integrate customer KMS for Private. hosted retains logs for X days by default but we can discuss extended retention or do a Private deployment for sensitive PHI. Dana, I'd love to follow up with your checklist — Jordan will send our security pack.
[06:44] Dana: yes please include KMS flow diagram and audit log schema.
[06:48] Maya: quick note on cost — if you run streaming with frequent small responses, cost is per token; batching multiple small prompts together reduces per-token overhead. Optimize will recommend batch sizes based on your observed sequence lengths.
[07:05] Alex: do you have an SDK for streaming reconnects? we use JS in the browser.
[07:10] Maya: yes we have SDK helpers and example client side code for SSE and WebSocket reconnection patterns. i'll drop links in chat.
[07:18] Jordan: ok i'm going to demo a simple sandbox run — spinning up a small chat that summarizes a mock encounter. starting request now.
[07:25] [LIVE DEMO: POST /v1/chat.generate stream=true]
[07:30] Maya (voice-over): you can see 3 chunk events arriving: 'The patient reports', 'a two-day history', 'of intermittent...' final event done: true. if the connection drops i can call the endpoint with the same idempotency key and the runtime will resume or return the cached final output.
[07:58] Sam: in your example, do you preserve KV cache across user sessions?
[08:03] Maya: KV cache is per-route and has configurable TTL; you can namespace per-user or per-tenant so it won't leak across sessions. for PHI, we suggest explicit namespace with customer-managed keys in Private.
[08:20] Alex: show us an example retry flow when network blips occur.
[08:24] Maya: demo reconnect: i kill the stream — the client sees aborted connection, retries with exponential backoff, then reconnects with same key and receives either resume or final. if resume isn't supported it returns a final cached output and we handle dedupe.
[08:45] Priya: any guidance on max in-flight requests? we expect 500 concurrent users during peak.
[08:50] Luis: for hosted API, start with rate limits per-token and per-minute; we can set custom quota and discuss Dedicated if you need predictable throughput. Dedicated gives you GPU pools so concurrency and tail latency are more predictable.
[09:07] Alex: ok that maps to our capacity question. can you send a cost projection for our 500 concurrent users with average 200 tokens per session?
[09:13] Jordan: yes i'll put together a worksheet — that's in the action items.
[09:18] Maya: last note — for safety/regression, run evals on a held set of prompts before model rollouts; the Console can alert on quality drop.
[09:29] Speaker 1: yep good idea
[09:31] Jordan: let's do quick recap and next steps. Maya will send the streaming retry doc and SDK links. I'll send pricing and the sandbox link. Sam will try the sandbox and report latency numbers by next Monday. Dana will review security pack and KMS flow.
[09:47] Alex: thanks, this was helpful. any other questions?
[09:51] Priya: none from me.
[09:53] Dana: no.
[09:55] Jordan: great, we'll follow up via email and calendar. thanks everyone.

End of transcript.
